text: Tidal Effects The measurement of ocean tides on the Ross Ice Shelf has previously been reported by Thiel and others (1960), Thiel (1960), and Bennett (1964). The proposal for RISP is to utilize available recording tidal gravimeters to provide a general description of variation of the amplitude and phase of the principal tidal harmonic constituents over the region. The Ross Ice Shelf provides a natural setting for an experimental study of the fluid dynamics associated with the tide in an embayment with a solid cover. Knowledge of the ocean tide will contribute to an understanding of the water circulation and bears directly on other proposed investigations to the extent that currents associated with the tide affect mass wastage of the base of the ice shelf and transport of marine organisms and sediment. Geology Primary information concerning the underlying geology will come from long seismic refraction shooting and regional gravity surveys. It has been suggested that there is a mean negative isostatic anomaly over the entire Ross Ice Shelf indicative of incomplete rebound after retreat of a grounded ice sheet. The regional gravity survey may also detect anomalous areas worthy of further study. It is recognized that long seismic refraction profiles will yield only indirect evidence on the thickness of sediment layers with wave velocities less than ice; however, information about upper crustal structure can be derived which will complement the Eltanin work in the Ross Sea.
